claim: A locomotive can weigh about a hundred tons (Siemens ACS-64: 98,000 kg / 217,000 lb)
source_quote: Weight 217,000 lbs 98000 kg
note: Owner's fixed first line (blueprint 6.3). 98 t metric, 108 US short tons: 'one-hundred-ton' is a round figure. Example loco on screen is generic, not branded.

claim: A train wheelset has two wheels fixed rigidly to one axle, so both turn together (no differential)
source_quote: a pair of railroad vehicle wheels mounted rigidly on an axle
note: Second source W: cylindrical treads impossible without skidding unless the wheels are independently mounted.

claim: Rounds curves at high speed and its wheels stay on the rails (on gentle curves the cone steers alone)
source_quote: On a curve it is possible for a coned wheelset to roll round the curve, by simply moving outwards
note: Owner chose this wording 2026-10-31 (replaces the blueprint's 'without ever derailing'). Derailment on curves is shown honestly in C17.

claim: On a bend turning the track through a right angle, the outer rail is about 2.4 m longer than the inner (any radius; contact points about 1.5 m apart)
source_quote: 2 * b0 * radians(90) with b0 = 0.75 m (NTNU worked example: b0 = 0.75 m)
note: Geometry: path difference = gauge-width x angle; b0 from N. On screen: MODEL.

claim: A car's differential lets the outer wheel turn faster than the inner one in a turn
source_quote: A differential allows the outer drive wheel to rotate faster than the inner drive wheel during a turn.

claim: Wheel treads are coned, about 1 in 20
source_quote: Most train wheels have a conical taper of about 1 in 20
note: Second: W 'restricting the equivalent cone angle of the wheel tread to either 1 : 20 or 1 : 40'.

claim: On a curve a coned wheelset shifts outward so the outer wheel rolls on a larger radius and it steers without slipping
source_quote: A coned wheelset can do this without axle slip if it shifts laterally.
note: Second: W 'roll round the curve, by simply moving outwards'; A 'effective guidance ... by varying rolling radii'.

claim: On a gentle curve the flanges need not touch the rail
source_quote: On a curve it is possible for a coned wheelset to roll round the curve, by simply moving outwards
note: Flange contact comes only when the curve is too sharp (C12). WIKI-WS: conicity gives less chance of flange contact.

claim: Lateral play before flange contact is about ±7 mm
source_quote: A flangeway clearance is provided so that the wheelset can move laterally within a distance of about ±7 mm
note: Standard gauge; Indian broad gauge has 19 mm total play new (IRIMEE): not used.

claim: At full shift (7 mm) on a 1:20 cone the two wheels differ in radius by about 0.7 mm
source_quote: 2 * (1/20) * 0.007 m = 0.70 mm (radius change per wheel = conicity x shift, definition lambda = delta r / y in N)
note: On screen: MODEL. Definition from N: 'lambda = delta r / y'.

claim: A bank card is about 0.76 mm thick
source_quote: four different sizes of identification cards with a nominal thickness of 0,76 mm
note: ISO/IEC 7810 (2003 edition; replaced 2019).

claim: A coned wheelset self-centers: drifting off-center changes the rolling radii so it steers back
source_quote: the effective diameters change in such a way as to decrease the curvature of the path
note: Second: A (kinematic oscillation about the centre).

claim: To steer round a 500 m curve the textbook wheelset (r0 0.5 m, b0 0.75 m, 1:20) must shift about 15 mm
source_quote: The wheelset must therefore shift about 15 mm outward to steer perfectly through this curve.

claim: With a 1:20 cone and ±7 mm play, clean rolling ends at about a 1 km radius (1,071 m); 1:40 about 2.1 km
source_quote: R = b0 r0 / (lambda y) = 0.75*0.5/(0.05*0.007) = 1071 m (formula y_R = b0 r0 / (lambda R) from N; clearance from W)
note: Model value; on screen labelled MODEL.

claim: On sharp curves the wheels slip and the flange contacts the rail
source_quote: if the curve is too sharp, the wheels will slip, flange contact will be made
note: Second: N, flange contacts the gauge corner of the high rail in tight curves.

claim: Curve squeal is widely attributed to stick/slip from lateral creepage of the tread on the top of the rail, not flange rubbing; the wheel vibrates (rings); the mechanism is still debated
source_quote: it is widely accepted that curve squeal arises from stick/slip behaviour due to lateral creepage of the wheel tyre on the top of the rail. The actual mechanism of the instability is however still a controversial topic.
note: VO says 'widely accepted', never 'proven'. Rudd discarded longitudinal creepage and flange rubbing as causes (same paragraph). 'Self-excited vibrations of the railway wheel' (abstract) = 'rings like a bell'.

claim: Nadal's formula gives how hard a flange can be pushed sideways relative to the wheel load before the wheel climbs; for typical flanges the limit is around 1 (0.86 at 60°, 1.22 at 70°, mu 0.35); beyond it the wheel can climb and derail
source_quote: For example, with mu=0.35: beta = 60 deg: (Y/Q)_Nadal ~ 0.86; beta = 70 deg: ~ 1.22
note: Second: IRIMEE 'THE PROCESS OF FLANGE CLIMBING DERAILMENT', Nadal's equation. Year: 1908 (IRIMEE) vs 1896 (other sources): VO says only 'more than a century ago'.

claim: The cone causes a sinusoidal side-to-side oscillation of the wheelset (overshoot and return)
source_quote: the effective diameters change in such a way as to decrease the curvature of the path
note: Second: A 'conicity of the wheelset has a serious side-effect which is usually called kinematic oscillation'.

claim: Engineers knew of the coned-wheel sway about two hundred years ago (George Stephenson by 1821)
source_quote: He knew that these coned wheels gave rise to lateral oscillations
note: 1821 to 2026 = 205 years: 'two hundred years ago'. Context sentence: when Stephenson began work on the Stockton and Darlington railway in 1821. Second: A 'This was observed by George Stephenson'.

claim: Klingel analysed the oscillation in 1883
source_quote: Klingel's famous model for the small oscillations of a single wheelset was published in 1883
note: Ref: Klingel, J., Organ fur die Fortschritte des Eisenbahnwesens 38, 113-123 (1883).

claim: Textbook wheelset: wavelength about 17 m; about 2.6 sways a second at 160 km/h
source_quote: L_K ~ 17 m ... If the same wheelset runs at 160 km/h, v=44.4 m/s and f_K ~ 2.6 Hz
note: Our model: 17.2 m, 2.58 Hz. VO: 'about two and a half'. Klingel's formula is an approximation (A).

claim: Below a critical speed the sway is damped out; above it hunting grows and can be violent, flanges striking the rails
source_quote: the motion can be violent, damaging track and wheels and potentially causing derailment
note: Second: W 'there is a speed at which the successive overshoots neither grow nor decay'; IRIMEE 'greater flange forces'.

claim: Critical speed falls as conicity rises: fast trains use flatter cones
source_quote: Most Important - Conicity / Inversely Proportional to Conicity
note: Second: IRIMEE 'For high speed - low 1 in 40 on high speed routes'; W 1:20 or 1:40.

claim: Japan's bullet trains used a standard wheel profile with a 1/40 conical tread (past tense)
source_quote: This wheel has the standard profile of Shinkansen with initially a 1/40 conical tread.
note: Tanifuji, JSME Trans. C (1988). Repository returned 503 on 2026-10-31; quote from the record's abstract as indexed. Second: WIKI-HO less-conical wheels on the Shinkansen. Re-open before lock.

claim: High-speed vehicles use stiff primary suspension and yaw restraint to resist hunting
source_quote: relatively high primary lateral and longitudinal suspension stiffnesses
note: Also 'rotational restraint between bogie and body'.

claim: Trade-off: steeper cone allows tighter curves (C14); flatter cone gives higher critical speed (C23)
source_quote: Inversely Proportional to Conicity
note: Curving side from the model (C14).

claim: On a curve the coned wheelset moves outward until its two rolling circles fit a cone with its apex at the centre of the curve
source_quote: by simply moving outwards so that the two rolling circles fit a cone with its apex at the centre of the curve
note: Signature 4.

claim: The sideways oscillation of a coned wheelset is called hunting
source_quote: a sustained lateral oscillation of a vehicle, which is termed hunting, can occur
note: Also A: 'When combined with creep, the resulting oscillation is called hunting.'

claim: At low speed the oscillation is damped and the wheelset returns to the centre
source_quote: At low speeds, following a disturbance, the wheelset oscillates, but the oscillation is damped
note: Wickens attributes the damping to creep forces; the VO says only 'damped out'.

claim: Stiff suspension that keeps axles straight for stability works against perfect steering in curves
source_quote: perfect steering would be achieved if each wheelset, in a bogie or vehicle, adopted a radial position on the curve
note: Same article: stability requirements prevent perfect steering (paraphrase from the fetch). Re-quote the exact stability sentence before lock.
